doc.title: Lionel Hampton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

title: Hiring Dinah Washington and Joe Williams at the Regal Theater
summary: Hampton notes he was the first Black musician in a white band, then tells how at Chicago's Regal Theater he renamed Ruth Jones as Dinah Washington and hired Joe Williams on the spot.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Joe Williams: the singer with Basie

blocks.x: I’m going to tell you about that deal. When I was looking for a girl singer, and I got to Chicago, the band had been popular, but the band was always popular because I was popular, and I could carry the band myself because I was the first black musician to play in a white band. See and Teddy Wilson was playing with Benny, but he used to play

when Benny used to take intermission, and no white musicians was on stage, then Teddy would play, by himself see? So I was the first one, legally to break that tradition down. But you know the funny thing about it, there wasn’t no black and white playing together no place. Not in pictures, moving pictures, not in baseball, or football, no kind of sports. The Benny Goodman quartet was the first mixed group and it was, you know? So I was playing in Chicago at the Regal Theater, that’s the black theater on the south side of Chicago, where all the big name black acts and name bands would play at. So Joe Glaser got there ahead of me, and a friend of his named Joe Sherman that owned the Sherman Bar where all the sailors from Great Lakes used to come to his place and drink, and it was 25 cents a beer, and hear jazz. At that time they had a great trumpet player that used to play with Earl “Fatha” Hines’ band, oh, what was that trumpet player’s name. If I called his name you would know it.
No, I’m sorry, but you were talking about Joe Williams.

Oh yeah, Joe Williams came into the story. So Joe Glaser came and he told me this friend, Joe Sherman that owned this Sherman Bar & Grill, he told him he was looking for a girl singer for me. So Joe Sherman said, “Well come down and I’ll have my girl in the washroom sing something. You’ll see how she sounds. She sounds pretty good to me.” And that’s what Joe said to Joe Glaser. And I’m trying to think of the trumpet player too that had the band, he had a really hot band, about six or seven pieces. So Joe Glaser went down that night and heard her sing. He came back and told me, “She sounded all right to me.” So Joe Glaser invited her to come out to the Regal Theater. And we used to do four shows out there at the Regal Theater, two in the afternoon and two at night. And we had people lined up two blocks to get in to the theater. But they didn’t have no place to go. Black people didn’t have no place to go for their own places, you understand? Those days for them, of course, they didn’t go downtown to the white theaters, and they came to the neighborhood theater, and they got big entertainment. Because all the big bands were out there, and also all the black entertainers, singers and dancers and so forth. So the girl from the washroom came out to the theater and sang for me, and I heard her sing, and I said she broke it up, with the crowd. I said to her, “I sure do like your singing.” I said, “Would you like to join the band?” And she said, “Yes, I’d like to join the band.” Naturally she would say it for we were the hottest band in the country at that time. And so I said, “Well tell me what’s your name?” She said, “My name is Ruth Jones.” I said, “I like your singing, but I don’t like that name.” I said, “Can I change your name?” She said, “I don’t care what you call me, as long as you give me the job to sing with you.” I said, “from now on your name is Dinah Washington.” Out of the clear blue sky I said

that. The guy that was standing next to me, because he was a friend of the manager of the Regal Theater where I was playing at, said, “oh, there goes my chance, I wanted to sing with the band.” So I said, “You can sing at the next show, because we’re going to do two matinees.” And I said, “What’s your name?” He said, “My name is Joe Williams.” I said, “Well okay, you can sing.” So I hired him and for two years I had Dinah Washington and Joe Williams for a boy and girl singer.
Yes it was. They’d sing everything off the map. Because they was great singers. So that’s the Joe Williams story.
